alt: A table of the four questions that test critical reading: Paper 1 Question 1 (4 marks), Paper 1 Question 4 (20 marks), Paper 2 Question 1 (4 marks) and Paper 2 Question 2 (8 marks). A bar shows that Paper 1 Question 4 equals the other three Paper 1 reading questions together. AO1 and AO4 carry most of the skill.
caption: Paper 1 Question 4 is the heaviest single test of critical reading.

after: ## Key idea 1: explicit, implicit and the inference chain
alt: Explicit information is stated, as in “The kitchen was empty.” Implicit information is suggested: a kettle “still ticking as it cooled” implies someone left in a hurry. An inference chain runs from a detail, to what it suggests, to why it matters to the question. Tentative verbs such as suggests and implies suit weaker evidence; shows and proves are for what is stated.
caption: Detail, then what it suggests, then why it matters, with verbs matched to the evidence.

after: ## Key idea 2: reading in different ways for different purposes
alt: Three panels. Scanning stays inside the named lines to pick out exactly what is asked. Skimming gives the overall shape of the text on a first read. Close reading gives slow, line-by-line attention to one section for evaluation.
caption: Scan for short questions, skim for shape, read closely to evaluate.

alt: Analysis asks how a method creates an effect; evaluation asks how well the writer achieves what a statement claims. The statement “lonely and frightened” is split into two claims: strong evidence for loneliness, weaker evidence for fear, and a hint of defiance, giving the judgement “mostly agree, with a qualification”.
caption: Split the statement into its claims and weigh the evidence for each.

after: ## Key idea 4: bias, evidence and unsupported claims
alt: Five warning signs: generalisation from one example, such as “every teenager I meet is glued to a screen”; anecdote presented as proof; loaded language such as “so-called experts”; selective evidence; and opinion stated as fact with no source or reason.
caption: Ask of every claim what supports it, then explain why it is slanted.

alt: Five steps of the model paragraph on Mara. It opens with the judgement “I partly agree”, infers she is stranded, gives two readings of the timetable detail, evaluates how the dead phone is withheld to reveal a bluff, and ends that she is frightened rather than helpless.
caption: Test the key word, read a detail two ways, and earn a qualified judgement.

alt: Four claims from the town-centre extract are sorted. The closed shops and the council survey are supported, by checkable fact and a named source. “Nobody under thirty shops locally any more” is an unsupported generalisation, and “Our town centre is dying” is a metaphor that sounds more certain than the evidence allows.
caption: Facts and named sources support a claim; generalisations and metaphors may not.
